title: Honda's Accidental Success in America
text:
In 1959 Honda sent a small team led by Kihachiro Kawashima to Los Angeles to open the American market. In interviews later collected by the management scholar Richard Pascale, the Honda men described how little their plan resembled what happened. They had little money and believed Americans wanted big motorcycles, so they concentrated on their larger 250cc and 305cc machines. They thought their small 50cc Supercub would look out of place in a country of big bikes.

The big bikes soon failed. Ridden hard and long on American highways, they leaked oil and their clutches broke down, and Honda had to ship them back to Japan for repair. Meanwhile the team had been using Supercubs to run errands around Los Angeles. People kept asking about them, and eventually a buyer from Sears called. Short of alternatives, Honda began selling the little bikes, not through motorcycle dealers but through sporting goods stores and other retailers.

The Supercub found a market of ordinary people who had never thought of buying a motorcycle. An advertising campaign launched in the early 1960s, built around the line "You meet the nicest people on a Honda", reinforced the image. Within a few years Honda was the leading motorcycle seller in the United States. Pascale published the account in 1984 to argue that business strategy is often discovered by learning from events rather than planned in advance.
lesson: Plans rarely survive contact with the market. Watch what is actually working, even when it contradicts your plan, and be willing to follow it.
people: Kihachiro Kawashima, Honda Motor Company, Richard Pascale
source: Richard T. Pascale (1984). Perspectives on Strategy: The Real Story Behind Honda's Success. California Management Review, 26(3)
caveat: The account rests on executives' recollections years later, and scholars still debate how much Honda's success was emergent rather than deliberate.
